title: Why this whale carcass is being dropped 40 feet into the ocean
summary: The whale's skeleton and soft tissues have been put into recycled netting and submerged 40 feet below the ocean surface as part of an effort to preserve it.

image.caption: The dead humpback whale is seen floating off the coast of Bowen Island after it was struck by a ferry. Now, its remains will be dropped into the ocean as part of an effort to preserve it. (Vivian Salama)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The whale's skeleton and soft tissues have been put into recycled netting and submerged 40 feet below the ocean surface as part of an effort to preserve it.
The humpback, named Notcho, washed up dead in Howe Sound after being struck by a ferry
A First Nation in B.C. is preserving the remains of a dead humpback whale that was struck by a ferry in Howe Sound back in October by submerging them in the ocean.
The whale, identified as Notcho (BCX1700), was struck by a B.C. Ferries vessel on Oct. 18 and was found floating a few days later off Gambier Island, roughly 30 kilometres from Vancouver.

Chairperson Sxwíxwtn Wilson Williams of the Squamish Nation said the recovery and preservation of the whale is one of the most significant marine mammal stewardship initiatives undertaken by the nation.
"The project has brought together community members, cultural knowledge holders, technical experts, and external partners," Williams said in a statement.
The nation, Fisheries and Oceans and the Canadian Coast Guard worked collaboratively to bring the dead whale to Squamish Nation’s Xwemelch’stn (Capilano) village.
The dead whale was found by the Grace Islands off B.C.'s coast, according to the Marine Education and Research Society (Emily Ashton)

"Throughout this process, our objective has been to ensure that decisions are guided by Squamish values, environmental stewardship, scientific best practices, and respect for the life of the animal," Williams said.
The whale skeleton and soft tissues were put into recycled netting and transported to Howe Sound near one of the nation’s traditional villages.
The nets were tied onto a line and submerged roughly 40 feet (12.19 metres) into the ocean.
Williams said once the flesh is fully removed from the skeletal remains, a diver will retrieve them. The bones will then be put in a location to dry out and be bleached by the sun.
The dead whale is seen floating on the shore near Burrard Inlet off Squamish Nation’s Xwemelch’stn (Capilano) village. (Squamish Nation)
The process will be regularly monitored by the nation to document the whale's natural decomposition, which is expected to take six months to a year.

Community workshops are being planned so First Nation members can process the remaining blubber, with processing set to focus on whale oil in traditional and contemporary applications, according to the nation.
Paul Cottrell, marine mammal co-ordinator with Fisheries and Oceans Canada said on Oct. 30 that whale carcasses are a very important part of the ocean’s food web.
"They're really islands of life in these deep ecosystems," Cottrell said.
First Nation to honour dead humpback whale struck by B.C. Ferries with cultural ceremony
There is often a desire to have a carcass decompose in the ocean, but Cottrell says it takes a lot of logistics and preparation.
Fisheries and Oceans Canada said an investigation into the death of the whale remains ongoing.

blocks.text: A necropsy was done on the whale, and DFO said its findings are still being assessed.
A cultural ceremony is being planned with cultural leaders, elders, knowledge holders and community members by the Squamish Nation.
